prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks first after reading all eight ballots. Four members put it first and six rank it in their top three, but I do not rest the case on that count. On the science, the magic-wavelength condition removes the light shift from the trap, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil broadening. That gives statistics, and therefore stability, that a single trapped ion cannot match. Katori proposed the concept and made the first demonstrations. Ye's group then showed the accuracy and stability at the 10^-18 level, including the many-body, Fermi-degenerate clock and millimetre-scale gravitational redshift. This is reproducible, quantitative work. Several independent laboratories now reach this regime and compare clocks routinely over fibre links. For me the real test is whether a result opens new ways of observing nature, and this one does: relativistic geodesy, searches for varying constants and dark-matter signatures, and a credible basis for redefining the second. The prize is clearly distinct from 2005 (the frequency comb) and 2012 (single-ion control), because it concerns a different route to precision, namely many neutral atoms in a lattice. Two names give the cleanest attribution of any entry on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit and overlap. Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Hollberg, Gill, the NIST ion-clock groups and the comb developers all contributed to the neighbouring steps, and a two-name award will look incomplete to some. A committee could also see optical clocks as an extension of the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes rather than a new discovery. The practical payoff, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened. Finally, the result is a measurement advance whose largest scientific returns (dark matter, constants, geodesy) are still prospective. I weigh measurement heavily, but I accept that this is the exact point on which colleagues who prefer discovery of new phenomena may disagree with me.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks atom interferometry (B004) third and values it as the cleanest demonstration of matter-wave interference, noting that Chu and Kasevich developed the light-pulse sensors and that Chu is not on the credited list.
responses.response: I ranked B004 second, so I share her view of its importance, and I accept that Chu not being on the supplied list makes the attribution difficult. That is the main reason I keep it as an alternative. With Pritchard, Bordé and Kasevich, plus Schmiedmayer's group, the credit cannot be assigned as cleanly as for the clocks. I also see a difference in the instruments. Field gravimeters and gradiometers exist, but the large-baseline fundamental tests that would justify a prize on discovery grounds are still being built, whereas clock comparisons at 10^-18 are already routine. I would not fight against B004 as a second part if we find a clean credited-name set, but I do not think it displaces B022.

responses.point: Pearce puts IceCube (B002) first as a purpose-built detector that opened a new observational window, with Halzen as the single credited person, and places the clocks second.
responses.response: I respect the argument that opening a new window is among the best forms of discovery, and I do not dismiss neutrino astronomy. But I find the evidence less mature. The diffuse flux is solid, while individual sources such as TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 sit at only a few sigma, as Danielsson also notes. The attribution is a larger problem. A single-name award for a collaboration of hundreds, with Botner, Karle, Spiering and others not credited, is hard to defend on this pack. The clock result by contrast is reproduced by several labs, with clear individual contributions. Pearce's own ranking of B022 second suggests we are closer than the first-place counts imply.

responses.point: Olsson ranks tunnel magnetoresistance (B038) first as an original, verified experiment with large technological effect (read heads, MRAM), with Miyazaki and Moodera as the natural original pair, and ranks the clocks third.
responses.response: I agree that TMR is solid, original experiments, and as an experimentalist I find the 1995 result and the MgO coherent-tunnelling follow-up convincing. My reservation is the neighbour effect. The committee would have to explain why it is distinct from GMR in 2007, since TMR is largely a refinement of spin-dependent transport in a related device. The attribution is also unsettled: Parkin, Yuasa and Djayaprawira reported giant MgO TMR almost at the same time, and not all are credited. I see more scientific novelty in being able to measure time at 10^-18 than in a better read-head sensor, though I accept that the impact on technology of TMR is larger today than that of clocks.

responses.point: Johansson ranks the clocks first on the clean physical idea and control of systematics, and the optical-lattice quantum simulation (B020) second, while declaring closeness to circuit QED (B014) at third.
responses.response: I agree with her on the clocks and her note that a redefinition of the second is a possibility but not a fact. On B020 I differ slightly. I rank it fourth because I think its achievements so far are methods rather than a decisive scientific result, such as a solved doped Hubbard model, and the five-name credit pool is a real problem since trimming it will exclude Cirac or Esslinger. I would also say that her disclosure on B014 is the right way to handle it; I would treat circuit QED on the science alone and note that the 2025 prize reduces room for a close relative.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues who prefer new phenomena over precision measurement will see optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether a two-name award for Katori and Ye is robust against the credit claims of Lemonde, Hollberg, Gill and the ion-clock groups, which I cannot verify beyond my own recollection.
Timing: whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before recognising the clocks.
Whether B004 can be given a clean credited-name set given that Chu is not in the supplied names.
statement.conflict_note: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD, and Jun Ye is a long-standing close collaborator of Hall at JILA, so there is a mild personal link to the B022 community. I do not have a direct collaboration or supervisory tie to Katori or Ye in my profile, but I flag it so the committee can judge whether it matters. I am also in the leadership of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (WACQT, Chalmers-led) and so have an institutional overlap with circuit QED (B014) and with Göran Johansson's home institution; I would recuse myself from any decision that depends on B014. My own field of rare-earth-ion quantum memories and slow-light work gives no direct connection to B022, B004 or B043.
